case_name: Isaac v. Guardian Capital Group, et al.
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Isaac v. Guardian Capital Group, et
al
.,

2004 BCSC 254

Date: 20040224

Docket:
S023850

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Stanley Russell Isaac

Plaintiff

And

Guardian Capital Group Limited,

3439666 Canada Inc.,

Worldsource Holdings Corp.,

Worldsource Financial Services Inc./

Services Financiers Worldsource
Inc.,

Worldsource Corporate Services Inc./

Services Administratifs Worldsource
Inc.,

Worldsource Securities Inc./

Valeurs Mobilières Worldsource Inc.,

Worldsource Insurance Agency Inc./

Agence d’Assurance Worldsource Inc.,

John Christodoulou and

Harold Hillier

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Melnick

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the plaintiff:

R.D.
Holmes

Counsel for the defendants:

R.B.
Fraser

J.
Berta

Date and Place of Hearing:

November
24, 25 and 26,

December
2, 3 and 5, 2003

Vancouver,
B.C.

[
1
]

Mr. Fraser brings the following two
applications:

1.

on behalf of two of the defendants for an order
striking out the statement of claim of the plaintiff, Stanley Russell Isaac
(“Mr. Isaac”), pursuant to Rule 19(24); and

2.

on behalf of the remaining defendants for an
order setting aside service, a declaration that the court has no jurisdiction
over them, a declaration and order that the court declines jurisdiction over
them, and an order that the proceedings against them be stayed pursuant to Rule
14(6) and 14(6.1).

I. BACKGROUND

[
2
]

Mr. Isaac advances a number of claims against
the defendants arising out of alleged contracts between him and some or all of
the defendants to establish a securities brokerage business in British
Columbia.  Two of the defendants, Worldsource Securities Inc. (“WS Securities”)
and Worldsource Corporate Services Inc. (“WS Corp.”) (collectively the “B.C. Defendants”),
are resident in British Columbia.  They bring an application under Rule
19(24).  The remaining corporate and individual defendants (collectively the “Ontario
Defendants”) have been served
ex juris
without leave pursuant to various
subrules in Rule 13(1).  They challenge the jurisdiction of the B.C. court
pursuant to Rule 14(6) and (6.1).

[
3
]

The allegations against the defendants include
breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation, defamation, wrongful
dismissal, constructive dismissal, quantum meruit and unjust enrichment.

II. RULE 19(24) APPLICATION

[
4
]

It is appropriate to deal with the Rule 19(24)
application first.  It is the B.C. Defendants’ position that Mr. Isaac’s
statement of claim is so confusing and it violates the rules for proper
pleadings to such an extent that they cannot properly respond to it.  They
submit that the whole of the statement of claim should be struck out and, essentially,
Mr. Isaac be required to start over.  It is Mr. Isaac’s position that the Rule
19(24) application “is simply wrong and is wholly without merit.”

A. Purpose of Pleadings

[
5
]

The B.C. Defendants argue that Mr. Isaac has
breached several elements of Rule 19.  In order to assess the persuasiveness of
their arguments I begin by characterizing the role of pleadings.

[
6
]

Mr. Justice Smith conveniently sets out the
purpose of pleadings in
Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia

(1998),
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, 25 C.P.C. (4th) 107 (B.C.S.C.) at page 109:

The ultimate function of pleadings is to
clearly define the issues of fact and law to be determined by the court.  The
issues must be defined for each cause of action relied upon by the
plaintiff.  That process is begun by the plaintiff stating, for each
cause, the material facts, that is, those facts necessary for the purpose of
formulating a complete cause of action:
Troup v. McPherson
(1965),
1965 CanLII 767 (BC SC)
, 53
W.W.R. 37 (B.C. S.C.) at 39.  The defendant, upon seeing the case to
be met, must then respond to the plaintiff's allegations in such a way that the
court will understand from the pleadings what issues of fact and law it will be
called upon to decide.

…. If the statement of claim is to serve the
ultimate purpose of pleadings, the material facts of each cause of action
relied upon should be set out in the above manner.  As well, they
should be stated succinctly and the particulars should follow and should be
identified as such:
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1988),
1988 CanLII 2832 (BC CA)
, 26
B.C.L.R. (2d) 349 (B.C. C.A.) at 353.

B. Standard on Rule 19(24)
Applications

[
7
]

While the B.C. Defendants complain of a variety
of breaches of Rule 19, the remedy for those breaches is in Rule 19(24). That
Rule reads as follows:

At any stage of a proceeding the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no
reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise
an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment or order the
proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the application
to be paid as special costs.

[
8
]

In practice, a party attacking pleadings often
makes reference to Rule 19(24) as a whole instead of relying on particular
subrules.  The B.C. Defendants in this case are guilty of such a broad-brush
approach.  Consequently, courts often gloss over which part of the rule they
are applying in their analysis.  Thus, it is useful to review how each rule has
been interpreted in order to be able to rely on the appropriate aspect of Rule
19(24).

[
9
]

Regardless of the subrule in 19(24) relied on,
the B.C. Court of Appeal in
Kripps v. Touche Ross & Co.
(1992),

1992 CanLII 923 (BC CA)
, 94 D.L.R. (4th) 284, makes clear at 289 that the court must decide an
application under Rule 19(24) on the pleadings either as they stand or as they
may be amended.

1. Rule 19(24)(a)

[
10
]

The standard on a Rule 19(24)(a) application is well established.  In

Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, the plaintiff
suffered illness from exposure to asbestos in the course of his work as an
electrician.  He accused several companies in the asbestos manufacturing and
use business of conspiracy to hide the fact that asbestos fibres could cause disease.
The defendant Carey brought an application under Rule 19(24)(a) to have the
conspiracy claim dismissed.  The Supreme Court of Canada noted at paragraph 12
that Rule 19(24) is a codification of the court’s inherent jurisdiction to stay
actions that are an abuse of process or that do not disclose a reasonable cause
of action.  After considering similar rules in England and in Ontario, as well
as jurisprudence from B.C. and the Supreme Court of Canada, the court set the
following test at page 980:

… assuming that the facts as stated in the
statement of claim can be proved, is it “plain and obvious” that the
plaintiff’s statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action?  As in
England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the
plaintiff should not be “driven from the judgment seat”.  Neither the length
and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the
potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the
plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case.  Only if the action is certain
to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the others listed in
Rule 19(24) of the British Columbia
Rules of Court
should the relevant
portions of a plaintiff’s statement of claim be struck out under Rule
19(24)(a).

[
11
]

Any doubt about whether or not a plaintiff has satisfied the test
set out in
Hunt
is to be resolved in the plaintiff’s favour:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.
v.
Canadian Jewish Congress

(1999),

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.).

2. Rule 19(24)(b)

[
12
]

The standard under Rule 19(24)(b) is also a “plain and obvious” one,
though it must be plain and obvious that the pleading is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious. Mr. Justice Romilly in
Citizens for
Foreign Aid
sets out a useful summary of the jurisprudence on this
subrule and parts of subrule 19(24)(c) at paragraph 47:

Irrelevancy and embarrassment are both
established when pleadings are so confusing that it is difficult to understand
what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),

1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C. S.C.)…. A pleading is "unnecessary" or
"vexatious" if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff's cause
of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan

(December 2, 1991), Doc. Vancouver C913631 (B.C. S.C.)…. A pleading is
"frivolous" if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the sense that
it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian
v. B.C. Rail Ltd.
(July 3, 1992), Doc. Prince George 20714 (B.C. Master).

3. Rule
19(24)(c)

[
13
]

Mr. Justice Hutcheon in

Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 (C.A.), sets out succinctly at page 147 what
constitutes an embarrassing pleading within the meaning of Rule 19(24)(c),
citing
Mayor of City of London v. Herner
(1914), 111 L.T. 512 (C.A.)
at 514:

… the allegations are so irrelevant that to
allow them to stand would involve useless expense, and would also prejudice the
trial of the action by involving the parties in a dispute that is wholly apart
from the issues.  In order that allegations should be struck out from
a defence upon that ground ... their irrelevancy must be quite clear and, so to
speak, apparent at the first glance.

4. Rule
19(24)(d)

[
14
]

This section is normally reserved for claims that clearly cannot
stand for such reasons as
res judicata
and issue estoppel:
World
Wide Treasure Adventures Inc. v. Trivia Games Inc.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 1428 (BC CA)
, 17 B.C.L.R.
(3d) 187 (C.A.).  Notwithstanding the fact that the B.C. Defendants have not
excluded reliance on this subrule, I do not consider that such issues arise in
this case.

C. Application of Rule 19(24)

[
15
]

Having regard to the kinds of complaints the B.C. Defendants
advance, Rule 19(24)(a) is, on the whole, the most applicable subrule.  Where I
believe another subrule is more appropriate, I will make that clear.

1. Breach of Contract and
Misrepresentation

[
16
]

Adopting the standard in
Hunt
, in order for me to
strike the plaintiff’s breach of contract and misrepresentation claims, it must
be plain and obvious that the statement of claim does not disclose a reasonable
cause of action on those grounds.

[
17
]

There is considerable confusion between what are alleged to be
clauses in the contract and misrepresentations.  I shall deal with them
together because it appears as though Mr. Isaac is relying on the same events
to show both breach of contract and misrepresentation.  I also note at the
outset that the B.C. Defendants complain that the supposed terms in paragraph
21 of the statement of claim are too vague to form the basis of a contract.  I
have not addressed that particular argument because WS Securities admits the
existence of a contract in its statement of defence.  While it may not agree as
to which terms are included in that contract or whether there was more than one
contract, it cannot now claim no reasonable cause of action because there is no
contract.

[
18
]

First, there is a measure of confusion with respect to the alleged
agreements.  “Agreement” and “Employment Agreement” are both defined terms in
the statement of claim.  However, paragraph 53 refers to “contract of
employment” and paragraph 54 refers to “various agreements”.  It is unclear if
these undefined terms refer to either both, or neither of the defined terms.

[
19
]

The second problem arising from the confusion and applicable to the
claims in contract is one of privity.  Throughout the statement of claim, Mr.
Isaac refers to the defendants as a group but nowhere does he specify who he
alleges are the actual parties to the contract(s).  While there is some jurisprudence
holding individuals who are not parties to a contract liable for breach of that
contract, without knowing which parties Mr. Isaac claims are the actual
parties, it is impossible to know what law applies here.  As well, without
knowing who are the parties to the contract, the defendants cannot know which
defences may be available to them.

[
20
]

A further problem is the making of what appear to be alternative
claims.  On the one hand Mr. Isaac is alleging that the defendants breached
fundamental terms and on the other hand he is claiming misrepresentation.  Mr.
Isaac is able to plead these in the alternative under Rule 19(8).  Subrules (7)
and (8) of Rule 19 provide:

(7) A party shall not plead an allegation of
fact or a new ground or claim inconsistent with the party’s previous pleading.

(8) Subrule (7) does not affect the right of a
party to make allegations in the alternative or to amend or apply for leave to
amend a pleading.

[
21
]

However, Mr. Isaac’s claims are not properly presented as
alternative positions.  For example, in paragraph 21, Mr. Isaac states that “[i]t
was a condition or fundamental term of the Agreement, and further, or
alternatively Mr. Hillier represented and warranted to the Plaintiff, that…”
followed by a list.  He also says in paragraph 40 that the defendants’ conduct
amounted to a repudiation of the Agreement.  But in paragraph 23 he says he
“reasonably relied upon these representations” and further, at paragraph 24, he
says that he agreed to forgo his salary in the first year “in reliance on the
conditions, fundamental terms, representations and warranties set out above”.  That
language could relate to a breach of warranty claim in contract or to negligent
misrepresentation.  Mr. Isaac’s primary position is not clear from these statements,
which makes it very hard to defend.

[
22
]

Similar criticisms apply to Mr. Isaac’s claims in wrongful and
constructive dismissal, which are also, properly, alternative positions.  He
seems to be alleging both in paragraph 41 but both cannot be true.  He adds
further allegations of wrongful dismissal in paragraphs 51-53.  Either he was
constructively dismissed before he was given notice of termination in March
2002 or he was wrongfully dismissed at that time.  While the problems with
alternative positions may not be enough on their own to justify striking the
statement of claim, they certainly add to the confusion with which the
statement of claim is replete.

[
23
]

There is a further problem in that the statement of claim is not
clear about how the defendants allegedly breached these various terms or how
the elements listed in paragraphs 21, 22, 24, 27 and possibly 39 turned out not
to be true.  In order for Mr. Isaac to make a proper claim in either contract
or in negligent misrepresentation, he needs to show that elements he understood
were going to be present did not in fact materialize.  He does set out some alleged
breaches at paragraph 31, which he relates to the delay in getting WS
Securities up and running, including claims that he was not given effective authority
and responsibility for the development of the business (para. 31(d)).  As well,
at paragraph 32, he alleges interference with an application for membership in
the Investment Dealers Association of Canada (the “IDA”), which presumably
affects the promise he alleges in paragraph 21(e): that the defendants would
take whatever steps were necessary to establish WS Securities.  That leaves
several claims without particulars as to the breaches on which Mr. Isaac relies
and some particulars hidden within broader allegations. There is no attempt to
itemize which actions relate to the repudiation of the contract alleged in
paragraph 40 or to the constructive dismissal alleged in paragraph 41.  A
blanket reference to all the fundamental breaches, breaches of warranty and misrepresentations
is not sufficient.

[
24
]

Also of concern is Mr. Isaac’s vague language when referring to the terms
or representations and their breach:

•

Paragraph 29: “The parties initially planned for
WS Securities to be operational by the end of June 2001, however, the
Defendants’ actions and inactions
including
those described below….”

•

Paragraph 31: “The Defendants fundamentally
breached the Agreement with the Plaintiff by causing serious delay to the
commencement of WS Securities operations and imposing a series of impediments
to the orderly and timely development of the business,
particulars of which
include but are not limited to the following
:

…

i)
such
further and other particulars as counsel may advise
.”

•

Paragraph 32: “Further, the Defendants
fundamentally breached the Agreement with the Plaintiff and their
representations and warranties to the Plaintiff by,
among other things
,
inappropriately interfering with the IDA membership application process.
Particulars of these breaches
include
the following….”

(Emphasis added)

[
25
]

Mr. Isaac should be specific both about the terms he complains were
breached and about the particulars of the breaches.  He is not entitled to add
other circumstances as he thinks fit forcing the B.C. Defendants to respond to
surprise allegations.

[
26
]

Because the factual matrix surrounding the contract or contracts is
unclear, the B.C. Defendants cannot properly respond to the claims of breach of
contract or misrepresentation.  While the B.C. Defendants take issue with many
of the alleged terms of the Agreement, the Employment Agreement or undefined
agreements, the fundamental problems in the statement of claim are the lack of
a clear picture as to: which terms belong to which agreement, how the terms
were breached, and who are the parties to the contracts.  Mr. Justice Smith in
Homalco

says at paragraph 11 that where confusing pleadings are “extremely difficult,
if not impossible, to answer” the defendant should not be required to do so.
That is the case here due to the uncertainty about the alleged agreements
themselves.

[
27
]

The B.C. Defendants also make a good point when they cite Madam
Justice Southin in
Cotton v. Wellsby
(1991),
1991 CanLII 5730 (BC CA)
, 59 B.C.L.R. (2d) 366
(C.A.) where she says at 373 that when a plaintiff files “a hopelessly
inadequate statement of claim, there is nothing upon which the trial judge can
concentrate his or her mind.”  Not only does the statement of claim in this
case confuse the defendants but it is likely to confuse the trial judge as
well.

[
28
]

However, all of that said, it is not “plain and obvious” that the
breach of contract claims will not succeed if Mr. Isaac is able to better
organize and particularize his allegations.  Although Mr. Isaac did not ask for
this relief the court has two options to correct defects in a statement of
claim relying on its inherent jurisdiction to control court proceedings: the
first is to order that Mr. Isaac provide further particulars of the claim under
Rule 19(16); the second is to strike the offending portion of the statement of
claim under Rule 19(24) but grant leave to amend it.  While there does not
appear to be a significant difference in result between these two options in
most cases, the former is less draconian than the latter; therefore, the latter
should be reserved for more egregious defects.

[
29
]

In my view, this is a case where the breach of contract claims
should be struck with leave to amend.  The claims are hopelessly confused and
intertwined, and although Mr. Isaac may have a reasonable cause of action once
the he reorganizes his pleadings, he does not have one now.

[
30
]

However, there is a fatal problem with Mr. Isaac’s negligent
misrepresentation claims.  The B.C. Defendants argue that Mr. Isaac’s claims in
paragraphs 21 and 22 are statements of intended future conduct and that those kinds
of representations are not actionable in tort.

[
31
]

In
MacMillan v. Kaiser Equipment Ltd.
,
2003 BCSC 672 (CanLII)
, [2003] B.C.J.
No. 1006 (S.C.) (QL), the plaintiff entered into two agreements with the
defendant saying he relied on various representations that he would receive future
equity ownership to compensate him for work done over and above his work as an
employee.  Madam Justice Allan says this at paragraph 83 about
misrepresentation claims, citing
Taylor v. Netron Inc.
,
[2002]
O.T.C. 574 (Sup. Ct. J.)
: “in order to establish a negligent misrepresentation,
the misrepresentation must be to existing facts, not future occurrences” (see
also
Williams v. Saanich School District No. 63

(1986),
1986 CanLII 1207 (BC SC)
, 37
C.C.L.T. 203 (B.C.S.C.), aff’d (1987),
1987 CanLII 2660 (BC CA)
, 14 B.C.L.R. (2d) 141 (C.A.)).  I note
that Madam Justice Allan in
MacMillan

dismissed the defendant’s
application to strike the statement of claim under Rule 19(24)(a) and (d).  However,
if the length of her reasons on this point is any indication, this was not the
focus of either party’s submissions.

[
32
]

All the representations in paragraphs 21, 22 and 24 refer to future
events.  As such the claim for negligent misrepresentation should be struck as
disclosing no reasonable cause of action.  As I mentioned above, Mr. Isaac
relies on the same allegations in breach of contract and in negligent
misrepresentation and I would limit him to pleading breach of contract for the
misrepresentations that concern him.  He will not have leave to amend the
negligence claim.  I have considered the B.C. Defendants’ argument that the “entire
agreement” clause in the agreement they admit exists precludes Mr. Isaac from
relying on the alleged misrepresentations in his claim for breach of contract.  However,
that argument is best left until Mr. Isaac remedies the confusion surrounding
the agreements.

[
33
]

Counsel for Mr. Isaac indicated during argument that Mr. Isaac was
not making a claim in fraudulent misrepresentation, something the B.C.
Defendants thought was being alleged because of his use of the terms “recklessness”,
“reckless” and “wanton” in paragraphs 33 and 54.  That is a further reason why
the misrepresentation claims should be struck in their entirety.  They are
properly struck as being embarrassing under Rule 19(24)(c):
Olsen v.
Behr Process Corp.
,
2003 BCSC 429 (CanLII)
, [2003] B.C.J. No. 627 (S.C.) (QL).

2. Defamation

[
34
]

Mr. Isaac claims that the communication of the termination of his
employment to the IDA was defamatory and injured his reputation.  In Raymond E.
Brown,
The Law of Defamation in Canada
, 2d ed. (Scarborough,
Ont.: Carswell, 1994) a defamatory statement is defined at page 54 as a false
statement to a person’s discredit.  While there are other elements to the tort,
that definition is sufficient to strike Mr. Isaac’s claim in this case.  Leaving
aside the factor that the statement has to discredit Mr. Isaac in some way,
which is far from clear to me, to be defamatory a statement has to be false.  In
other words, truth is an absolute defence.  In this case, the fact that Mr.
Isaac was terminated from his position as an investment advisor was a true
statement and cannot be defamatory. This makes it plain and obvious that the
plaintiff’s defamation claim is not a reasonable cause of action and it is
properly struck.

[
35
]

Further, Mr. Isaac has also failed in his obligation to plead the
particulars of his defamation claim. If he does not set out the precise words
complained of, the claim may be struck out under Rule 19(24)(a):
Shannon
v. King
,
1931 CanLII 325 (BC CA)
, [1931] 4 D.L.R. 438 (B.C.C.A.).  The exception to this
requirement is where the plaintiff does not know and cannot know the exact
defamatory words until he can extract them from the defendants on discovery,
such as where only the defendants were present when the words were spoken:
Bulkley
Nechako Cable Vision Ltd. v. CKPO Television Ltd.
(1982),
1982 CanLII 759 (BC SC)
, 37 B.C.L.R.
23 (S.C.). However, the plaintiff is not relieved from his obligation to plead
particulars where he can determine the precise words by investigating:
Bulkley
Nechako
.  This is the case here. Whether the communication was oral or
by letter, someone at the IDA could surely tell Mr. Isaac in precise terms what
was said about his termination.  There is no indication in the pleadings that Mr.
Isaac has attempted to ascertain the precise words.  This is a further ground
upon which I would strike the defamation claim.

[
36
]

The B.C. Defendants made much of the fact that they could not be
liable in defamation because a Ms. Richard was the one who sent the letter to
the IDA.  However, Rule 19(27) indicates that no evidence is admissible where an
application is made under Rule 19(24)(a).  The claim that Ms. Richard sent the
letter is not in any of the pleadings but is a statement in her affidavit,
which is inadmissible.  In any event, the B.C. Defendants do not need another
ground on which to strike out the defamation claim since they can rely on the
two grounds I mentioned above.  I would not grant leave to amend this claim.
Unless Mr. Isaac can plead some other untrue statement
that is alleged to be defamatory, I would not grant leave to amend this claim.

3. Unjust Enrichment

[
37
]

The leading Canadian cases in unjust enrichment are
Pettkus v.
Becker
,
1980 CanLII 22 (SCC)
, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 834 and
Peter v. Beblow
,
1993 CanLII 126 (SCC)
, [1993] 1
S.C.R. 980. Madam Justice McLachlin in
Peter v. Beblow
sets out
the test for unjust enrichment in this way at page 987:

An action for unjust enrichment arises when
three elements are satisfied:  (1) an enrichment; (2) a corresponding
deprivation; and (3) the absence of a juristic reason for the
enrichment.  These proven, the action is established and the right to
claim relief made out.

[
38
]

A claim in unjust enrichment exists where there is no contract on
which to base one’s right; if there is a contract then the much easier route is
to sue for breach of contract. Therefore, I will assume that Mr. Isaac has no
enforceable contract on which to rely.  This makes the unjust enrichment claim
an alternative claim to breach of contract.

[
39
]

The element of benefit is of little trouble in this case. Though WS
Securities apparently did not survive for long, Mr. Isaac allegedly did work to
start the business, drew up a business plan, organized the office space and
tried to recruit staff.  This provided WS Securities with a benefit.  However,
it is unclear whether any other defendant received a benefit. Further, the
corresponding detriment is problematic.  While Mr. Isaac allegedly spent time
working to develop the brokerage business, he does not plead that he was not
compensated for his work properly or at all. This is a significant gap in the
pleadings and the existence of the claim requires this factor; without it there
is no reasonable cause of action.  I order the unjust enrichment claim struck
but grant Mr. Isaac leave to amend this claim.  Because of the gravity of the
omission, more detail should be added by amendment, not with particulars.

4. Quantum Meruit

[
40
]

The Dictionary of Canadian Law
, 2d
ed. defines “quantum meruit” thus, relying on the decision of Madam Justice
Rowles in
Gill v. Grant

(1988), 30 E.T.R. 255 (B.C.S.C.)
:

…. In a contractual setting, remuneration is
said to be paid on a quantum meruit basis when, although a valid contract is
found to exist in fact and law, there is no clause spelling out in express
terms the consideration for the contract. In such circumstances, the courts
award reasonable remuneration to the person who has rendered the services.

[
41
]

Therefore, Mr. Isaac must show that there was a contract in
existence but that his remuneration was not expressly set out in that contract.
In this case, his ability to do so depends on the particularization of the
contract on which he is basing his claim for quantum meruit.  It also depends
on a finding that the term setting out his compensation, that he alleges was
included in the contract in paragraph 24 of the statement of claim, was not so
included; it is, therefore, properly an alternative position to his claim for
breach of contract.

[
42
]

There is little doubt that Mr. Isaac can properly plead quantum
meruit in these circumstances (assuming as I must at this stage that the facts
pleaded about his work to get WS Securities started are true) if he can point
to a particular contract and if he can show that he did not receive reasonable
compensation.  Unfortunately, Mr. Isaac has done neither here. He does not
specify the contract to which this claim applies and nowhere in the pleadings
does he say that he did not get any or got insufficient compensation for his
work to develop WS Securities, the same impediment to his claim in unjust
enrichment.

[
43
]

In this instance, once Mr. Isaac properly pleads breach of contract one
hopes that the particulars he pleads will be sufficient to indicate which
contract he is relying on for his quantum meruit claim.  But, as mentioned in
the section on unjust enrichment, because of the importance of the detail about
his not having received any or enough compensation, he should amend the
pleadings to include such a statement.  The quantum meruit claim is struck with
leave to amend.

5. Paragraph 11

[
44
]

While not alleging a cause of action, paragraph 11 pleads that at
all material times all defendants acted as the authorized employee, agent,
partner, joint venturer or representative of the others; that each held himself
or itself out as being able to represent and bind the others; that they all had
knowledge of the acts and omissions of the others; and that they acted jointly
and in concert with the others in committing the various wrongs against the
plaintiff.  With this paragraph, Mr. Isaac is presumably attempting to claim
that all defendants are jointly liable; however, as Mr. Fraser rightly points
out, because of the wording, Mr. Isaac is making the illogical claim that
corporations are employees or representatives of individuals.  That cannot be
so and it renders the claims in the paragraph suspect on their face. Also, Mr.
Isaac does not plead, as he must under Rule 19(9.1), any material facts to
indicate how these legal relationships were created or how they functioned.

[
45
]

A subsidiary issue is Mr. Isaac’s having referred to the defendants
as a group throughout the statement of claim, an approach likely related to the
language in paragraph 11.  It is unclear when he makes his various allegations
whether the defendants are accused of breaching contract(s) or of being liable
in unjust enrichment or quantum meruit because of their own actions or because
they are vicariously or jointly liable due to the actions of another party or
parties.  I discussed this problem above as it relates to the contract claims
specifically but it is problematic for all claims. It is possible that Mr.
Isaac could be making alternative claims but he has not made this clear.  This
leaves the defendants in the unworkable position of having to defend the
actions of an unknown or undefined party.

[
46
]

Paragraph 11 is rightfully characterized as embarrassing and should
be struck under Rule 19(24)(c). I give Mr. Isaac leave to amend this paragraph
on the following conditions: that he plead the material facts necessary to
support the legal relationships he maintains existed; that he specify which
defendants are parties to the contract(s); that he outline for each cause of
action which defendants are responsible for direct actions and which are
vicariously or otherwise liable; and that he be clear when he is advancing
alternative claims.

D. Conclusion on Rule 19(24)
application

[
47
]

As is evident from the above analysis, Mr. Isaac’s statement of
claim is so confusing and so replete with problems that it should be almost totally
redrafted.  While some paragraphs, such as the introductory paragraphs, are not
offensive, it is a task beyond what can be expected of the court to edit it any
further than I have already done.  Thus, the entire statement of claim should
be struck.  I would, however, grant leave to Mr. Isaac to file a new
(essentially totally amended) statement of claim except for those claims for
which I have not granted leave to amend.  In other words, he may advance claims
in breach of contract, unjust enrichment and quantum meruit.

II. RULE 14(6) APPLICATION –
JURISDICTION

[
48
]

In undertaking this analysis, I proceeded on the basis that the
former Rule 14 applies to these proceedings rather than the amended Rule 14.
In any event, neither side made an issue of it.

[
49
]

There is one very real problem with the jurisdiction application.  Without
setting out the law at this point, it will suffice to say that as part of my
analysis I am required to determine if Mr. Isaac has a good arguable case
against the Ontario Defendants.  It is impossible to determine whether Mr.
Isaac has a good arguable case on pleadings that have yet to be reformulated.
Mr. Isaac may or may not choose to join some or all of the Ontario Defendants
in his amended statement of claim.  He may or may not succeed in properly
describing his claims the next time, so that he may again face a Rule 19(24)
argument from the B.C. Defendants before the court can consider the Ontario
Defendants’ jurisdiction arguments.

[
50
]

Further, Mr. Isaac’s claim that the defendants are jointly liable
because of relationships of agency, employment, joint venture, partnership etc.
may turn out to have a legal basis once he amends his pleadings and it would be
premature to decide that the Ontario Defendants could not be parties before Mr.
Isaac’s claims are clear.

[
51
]

The same problem presents itself in any attempt to determine whether
this court has jurisdiction over the Ontario Defendants.  Thus, the application
of the Ontario Defendants will have to be considered after Mr. Isaac delivers a
properly drafted statement of claim setting out his claims in clear and
comprehensible form, including what he alleges are the relationships between
him and the various defendants.

[
52
]

I will remain seized of this matter for the limited purpose of
considering any further application with respect to an amended statement of
claim, including the question of jurisdiction.

IV. COSTS

[
53
]

The defendants are entitled to the costs of this application in any
event of the cause, payable as a condition to filing a new statement of claim.
However, I will not consider fixing costs at a rate other than Scale 3 without
the receipt of argument.  There is liberty to present such argument at a time
to be arranged if the defendants still wish to pursue other than normal costs.

[
54
]

I also observe that it was reasonable for the Ontario Defendants to
bring on their application with respect to jurisdiction, even if I was ultimately
unable to deal with it due to the result of the application of the B.C.
Defendants.  They are, therefore, not to be penalized in the form of costs for
having done so.
